sections.title: The state that was born fighting for a city
sections.intro_md:
On 21 November 1955, a crowd marched towards the Bombay legislature at Flora Fountain, in the middle of the city's banking district. They wanted one thing: a Marathi-speaking state with **Bombay as its capital**. Delhi instead proposed a bilingual Bombay State, and some wanted the city run separately, because its money was largely Gujarati and Parsi while its workers were largely Marathi.

The police fired. Over the next months of the Samyukta Maharashtra agitation, about **106 people** were killed. In the 1957 elections the movement's alliance won 101 of 133 seats in the Marathi region, and Delhi gave way. On **1 May 1960** Bombay State was split into Maharashtra and Gujarat, and Bombay stayed with Maharashtra.

That is the paradox to hold all day. Maharashtra is India's richest state, the home of its stock market, its film industry and its busiest port. It is also the land of Shivaji's forts and of deeply distressed cotton farmers. The state exists because people died to keep a city.

spotlights.name: Hutatma Chowk
spotlights.spot_it: A bronze man and woman holding up a flame on a stone plinth, a few metres from the white Victorian Flora Fountain.
spotlights.story_md: The square was built as a monument to empire: Flora Fountain, carved from imported Portland stone in 1864 and named after the Roman goddess of spring. After the 1955 and 1956 firings, it was renamed **Hutatma Chowk**, Martyrs' Square. The memorial shows a worker and a farmer raising a torch together, the two classes the movement claimed to speak for. Each 1 May, Maharashtra Day, the Chief Minister lays a wreath here. Most office workers who cross it every day still call it Flora Fountain, which is the whole history of Mumbai in two names.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the founding site of the modern state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Roman goddess and 106 martyrs share one traffic island.

sections.title: Maharashtra in numbers
sections.intro_md:
Maharashtra covers **307,713 km²**, India's third-largest state, about the size of Italy. Census 2011 counted **11.24 crore** people, second only to Uttar Pradesh; the 2025 estimate is close to 12.9 crore. Almost half of them live in towns and cities, far above the national average, and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region alone holds more than 2 crore.

It is the largest state economy in India. Gross state domestic product was about **₹51 lakh crore in 2025-26** (revised estimate), roughly 13 to 14% of India's GDP. Per person it ranks only around 12th: the wealth sits in the Mumbai-Pune-Nashik triangle, while Vidarbha and Marathwada lag.

The state has **36 districts** in six revenue divisions: Konkan, Pune, Nashik, Aurangabad (now Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar), Amravati and Nagpur. It sends **48 MPs** to the Lok Sabha, second only to Uttar Pradesh. Mumbai is the capital; **Nagpur is the winter capital**, where the legislature meets each December under the 1953 Nagpur Pact.

spotlights.name: Marine Drive
spotlights.spot_it: A 3.6 km curve of road along Back Bay, lined with Art Deco buildings; at night the streetlights read as a string of pearls.
spotlights.story_md: Marine Drive sits on land that was sea a century ago. It was reclaimed in the 1920s, and the buildings facing the bay form one of the largest groups of Art Deco architecture in the world, part of the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai that UNESCO listed in 2018. From the hills of Malabar at night the lights trace a curve that Mumbaikars call the **Queen's Necklace**. On monsoon high-tide days, waves clear the sea wall and soak the promenade, and half the city goes to watch.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the city's front room, where Mumbai goes to sit by the sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: The necklace was made from mud dumped into the sea.

sections.title: Basalt, monsoon and a meteorite
sections.intro_md:
Almost all of Maharashtra stands on **Deccan Trap basalt**, lava that poured out in vast floods about 66 million years ago, around the time the dinosaurs died. The layers cooled into the flat-topped, step-sided hills seen everywhere in the state.

The state has three bands. The **Konkan** is a narrow strip of coast, 30 to 60 km wide, wet, green and cut by short rivers. Behind it the **Sahyadri**, the northern Western Ghats, rises like a wall; the highest point is Kalsubai at 1,646 m. East of the wall lies the **Deccan plateau**, drier and tilting gently towards the Bay of Bengal, which is why the big rivers (the Godavari, the Krishna, the Bhima) all rise near the Arabian Sea and flow the other way across India.

The Ghats catch the monsoon. Mahabaleshwar gets over 5,000 mm of rain a year; parts of Marathwada, only 250 km east, get under 700 mm and face drought in bad years.

spotlights.name: Konkan Kada, Harishchandragad
spotlights.when: Deccan Traps, about 66 million years old
spotlights.spot_it: A concave cliff that curls over like a breaking wave, dropping hundreds of metres into the Konkan below.
spotlights.story_md: At the western edge of Harishchandragad fort the plateau simply ends. Konkan Kada is an overhanging, crescent-shaped basalt wall, often quoted at around 1,200 m above sea level with a sheer drop of several hundred metres. In the monsoon, clouds boil up from the valley; on some days trekkers see a circular rainbow, the Brocken spectre, with their own shadow inside it. On windy days, light objects thrown off the edge are said to blow back up. The cliff is the cleanest view in the state of what the Sahyadri is: one long lava escarpment facing the sea.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows why the Ghats split Maharashtra into a wet coast and a dry plateau.
spotlights.memory_hook: A frozen wave of lava, 66 million years old, still breaking over the Konkan.

spotlights.name: Lonar crater lake
spotlights.spot_it: A near-perfect round bowl, 1.8 km across, with a green salt lake at the bottom and ruined temples on its rim.
spotlights.story_md: A meteorite hit the Deccan basalt and left a crater 1.8 km wide and about 150 m deep. Lonar is often described as the only known large impact crater formed entirely in basalt, which makes it a stand-in for craters on the Moon and Mars; NASA and Indian scientists study it for that reason. The lake has no outflow, so it is both salty and strongly alkaline, with a pH near 10. In June 2020 it turned pink in a few days, as falling water raised the salt level and salt-loving microbes bloomed. Its age is disputed: about 52,000 years by one method, about 570,000 by another.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a planetary science laboratory in the middle of a farming district.
spotlights.memory_hook: A stone from space, a lake that turned pink overnight.

spotlights.name: Kaas plateau
spotlights.spot_it: A flat-topped hill carpeted in purple, yellow and white flowers for a few weeks after the monsoon.
spotlights.story_md: For most of the year Kaas is a bare laterite tableland at about 1,200 m. Then, after the rains, it erupts. More than 850 species of flowering plants have been recorded on about 10 km², many of them tiny and short-lived because the soil is only a few centimetres deep. Dozens grow nowhere else. Kaas became part of the Western Ghats UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, and the forest department caps visitors to protect it. Locals call the yellow Smithia bigemina 'Mickey Mouse' and other flowers 'Donald Duck' for their shapes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how much life the thin soil of the Sahyadri holds.
spotlights.memory_hook: For four weeks a year, a bare rock turns into a flower show.

spotlights.name: Tadoba Andhari Tiger Reserve
spotlights.spot_it: Teak and bamboo forest around a lake, and one of the most reliable places in India to see a wild tiger.
spotlights.story_md: Tadoba was declared a national park in 1955, Maharashtra's oldest and largest. It takes its name from Taru, a local deity, and the Andhari river. The reserve covers about 1,728 km² of dry teak forest and bamboo in Chandrapur district, a coal-mining area, so tigers here share the landscape with open-cast mines and 41,000 people in and around the reserve. Human-tiger conflict in Chandrapur is among the worst in India: villagers die each year in tiger attacks while collecting firewood or tendu leaves. Tourists, meanwhile, come because sightings are frequent.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the heart of Vidarbha's tiger country, and of its hardest conservation questions.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tigers next to coal mines: Tadoba is wild India in an industrial district.

spotlights.name: Trimbakeshwar and the source of the Godavari
spotlights.spot_it: A black stone temple with a tall ribbed spire below the Brahmagiri hill; a square stepped tank, Kushavarta, nearby.
spotlights.story_md: The Godavari, India's second-longest river, rises on Brahmagiri hill above Trimbak, only about 80 km from the Arabian Sea, and then runs about 1,465 km east to the Bay of Bengal. Pilgrims call it the Dakshin Ganga, the Ganga of the south. Trimbakeshwar temple, rebuilt by the Peshwa Balaji Bajirao in the 18th century, is one of the twelve jyotirlingas of Shiva; its linga is unusual for having three small faces for Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. Every 12 years the Simhastha Kumbh Mela is held here and at Nashik. The next is due in 2027.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties Maharashtra's geography to its faith: the river that crosses India starts here.
spotlights.memory_hook: A river that starts 80 km from one sea and ends in the other.

sections.title: Caves before kings
sections.intro_md:
Maharashtra has more rock-cut caves than any other part of India; most estimates put the majority of the country's known caves here. The basalt was the reason. It is hard enough to hold fine detail but even enough to carve, and the trade routes between the western ports and the Deccan passed through ghats where merchants, monks and kings paid for shrines.

The **Satavahanas**, who ruled from Pratishthana (today's Paithan) from about the 1st century BCE, controlled those routes. Under them and their successors, Buddhist monks cut prayer halls and monasteries at Bhaja, Karla, Nashik and Ajanta. Later dynasties, the **Vakatakas**, the **Rashtrakutas** and the Kalachuris, carved Hindu and Jain temples into the same rock at Ellora and Elephanta.

Three of Maharashtra's World Heritage Sites (Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta) are caves. Together they show 1,500 years of Indian art in one region, and they explain why Maharashtra's oldest written history is literally on its walls.

spotlights.name: Naneghat inscription
spotlights.spot_it: A rock-cut room at the top of a steep mountain pass, its back wall covered in lines of early Brahmi letters.
spotlights.story_md: Naneghat was a toll pass on the trade road from the coast at Kalyan up to the Satavahana capital. In a cave at the top, a queen, **Naganika**, had a long inscription cut listing the grand Vedic sacrifices her family had performed and the gifts they paid for them: thousands of cows, horses, elephants and coins. Scholars value it for two reasons: it is one of the earliest records of the Satavahanas, and it contains some of the oldest known forms of the numerals that became our 1 to 9. A large stone pot at the pass is said to have collected tolls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Maharashtra's written history, and an early form of our number signs, begins.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen's receipt for a sacrifice, carved at a toll booth 2,000 years ago.

spotlights.name: Karla Great Chaitya
spotlights.when: About 1st century BCE to 1st century CE
spotlights.spot_it: A huge horseshoe-shaped window over a rock-cut hall, with wooden ribs still arching across the ceiling inside.
spotlights.story_md: The Great Chaitya at Karla is the largest rock-cut Buddhist prayer hall in India, about 40 m long. Inside, two rows of pillars topped with carved elephants and riding couples lead to a stupa. The curved teak ribs on the ceiling are thought to be original, which would make them about 2,000 years old: wood that has survived because it is shielded from rain. Inscriptions record donors, including Greek traders (Yavanas) and a merchant from far-off places. Today a Hindu shrine to Ekvira Devi, goddess of the Koli and Agri communities, stands at the cave mouth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how rich the Deccan trade was, and how faiths layer on the same rock.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cathedral cut from one rock, with 2,000-year-old wooden ribs.

spotlights.name: Ajanta caves
spotlights.when: 2nd century BCE and about 460 to 480 CE
spotlights.spot_it: Thirty caves cut into a horseshoe bend of a river gorge; inside, painted walls of princes, dancers and the lotus-holding Bodhisattva.
spotlights.story_md: Ajanta was carved in two bursts: around the 2nd century BCE, and again in a short, intense period around 460 to 480 CE under the Vakataka king Harishena. Then it was abandoned and the jungle grew over it. On 28 April 1819 a British cavalry officer, **John Smith**, out hunting a tiger, was shown the entrance to Cave 10. He scratched his name and the date across a painting, and it is still there. The paintings, mostly Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives, are the largest surviving body of ancient Indian wall painting. The Padmapani in Cave 1 is the most reproduced.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the reference point for classical Indian painting.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tiger hunter found the greatest paintings in India, and signed one.

spotlights.name: Kailasa temple, Ellora Cave 16
spotlights.spot_it: A full multi-storey temple, with towers, bridges and life-size elephants, standing in a pit cut down into a cliff.
spotlights.story_md: Kailasa is not built. It was carved downward out of a single mass of basalt, starting from the top of the hill. Carvers cut three trenches to isolate a block, then shaped a complete temple from it: shrine, hall, gateway, bridges, two free-standing pillars and two stone elephants. The tower rises 32.6 m above the courtyard. It is attributed to the Rashtrakuta king **Krishna I**, around 756 to 773 CE. One estimate is that 250 workers could have finished it in about five and a half years; others think it took much longer. Ellora's 34 caves hold Buddhist, Hindu and Jain shrines side by side.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the largest monolithic rock-cut structures in the world, and a lesson in subtraction.
spotlights.memory_hook: They built a temple by taking away a mountain.

spotlights.name: Elephanta Trimurti
spotlights.spot_it: A colossal three-headed Shiva bust in a dark cave hall on an island in Mumbai's harbour.
spotlights.story_md: An hour by ferry from the Gateway of India, the main cave on Gharapuri island holds the **Sadashiva**, a three-faced Shiva more than 5 m tall. The central face is calm, the left is fierce, the right is gentle and feminine: creation, destruction and preservation in one stone. The Portuguese named the island Elephanta after a large stone elephant near the landing; it was later moved to the city and now stands in Jijamata Udyan, Byculla. Portuguese soldiers are said to have used some sculptures for target practice. The caves have been a World Heritage Site since 1987.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the masterpieces of Indian sculpture, inside the limits of Mumbai.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three faces, one god, a commuter ferry ride from the city.

sections.title: Yadavas, sultans and the fort that swallowed Delhi
sections.intro_md:
From about 1187 the **Yadava** kings ruled the Marathi country from Devagiri, a cone-shaped hill near today's Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Their court sponsored the first great Marathi literature. In 1296 Alauddin Khalji's army raided Devagiri, and by 1318 the Yadavas were finished.

Then came one of history's strangest decisions. In 1327 Sultan **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** ordered the capital of the Delhi Sultanate moved to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, the City of Fortune. Much of Delhi's elite was marched south, and a few years later the order was reversed. Those who stayed helped seed the Dakhni language.

The **Bahmani** sultanate (1347) and its successors, the Nizam Shahi of Ahmadnagar and the Adil Shahi of Bijapur, ruled the plateau for the next 300 years. Marathi families such as the Bhonsles served them as commanders. Persian ruled the offices; Marathi ruled the villages.

spotlights.name: Daulatabad fort (Devagiri)
spotlights.spot_it: A cone-shaped hill with sheer scarped sides, a moat, and a slim 30 m tower, the Chand Minar, near the gate.
spotlights.story_md: Devagiri's builders cut the lower slopes of the hill into a vertical wall so nobody could climb it. The only way up is through a twisting tunnel in the rock, once fitted with iron grates where defenders could light fires to fill it with smoke. A moat once held crocodiles, the story goes. Tughlaq's 1327 move of his capital here is remembered as a byword for a brilliant idea badly executed. The **Chand Minar**, a victory tower of about 30 m, was added by the Bahmanis in 1435.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where north Indian Islamic power first sat in the Marathi heartland.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sultan marched Delhi 1,100 km south, then marched it back.

spotlights.name: Bibi Ka Maqbara
spotlights.spot_it: A white domed tomb with four minarets in a walled garden, smaller and slimmer than the Taj Mahal it imitates.
spotlights.story_md: Aurangzeb's son Azam Shah built this tomb for his mother, **Dilras Banu Begum**, in Aurangabad in the 1660s. It is called the 'Taj of the Deccan' because it copies the Taj Mahal's plan, but it cost a fraction as much. Only the dome and lower panels are marble; the rest is basalt and brick finished with fine lime plaster polished to look like stone. Seen side by side, the two tombs show the Mughal treasury shrinking in a single generation as Aurangzeb poured money into his long Deccan wars against the Marathas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Mughal empire's footprint in Maharashtra, and a snapshot of its strain.
spotlights.memory_hook: The poor man's Taj: marble on the top, plaster underneath.

compare.difference: Same plan and four minarets, but a much smaller dome and mostly plaster rather than solid marble.

sections.title: Shivaji and the Maratha century
sections.intro_md:
In 1630 a boy named **Shivaji** was born at Shivneri fort near Junnar to Shahaji Bhonsle, a commander of the Bijapur sultanate, and Jijabai. By his late teens he was seizing hill forts around Pune. By his death in 1680 he had built an independent kingdom, been crowned Chhatrapati, and fought the Mughal empire, the strongest power in Asia, to a standstill in the Sahyadri.

His method was the land itself: about 300 forts on ridges and islands, a light cavalry that raided and vanished, and a navy to hold the Konkan coast. A council of eight ministers, the Ashta Pradhan, ran the state.

After his death the Mughals fought a 27-year war to crush the Marathas and failed. In the 18th century the **Peshwas** ruled from Pune and Maratha armies reached Delhi and Attock. The defeat at Panipat in 1761 broke that momentum, and the British ended Peshwa rule in 1818. In July 2025, twelve Maratha forts, eleven of them in Maharashtra, were added to UNESCO's World Heritage list as the **Maratha Military Landscapes of India**.

visual.title: The 12 forts of the Maratha Military Landscapes (UNESCO, 2025)

spotlights.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded man in a tall turban with a sarpech, a pointed beard and a sword; statues show him on a rearing horse.
spotlights.story_md: Shivaji's story is told in a handful of scenes every Maharashtrian child knows. In 1659 he met the Bijapur general **Afzal Khan** at Pratapgad, each with a hidden weapon, and killed him with steel tiger claws, the wagh nakh. In 1663 he raided the Mughal governor Shaista Khan's bedroom in Pune; the governor escaped by losing his fingers. In 1666, held under guard in Agra by Aurangzeb, he escaped, by legend hidden in baskets of sweets. He was crowned at Raigad on **6 June 1674**. Historians debate many details, but not his scale: he made a kingdom out of hill country.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the founding figure of Maratha and Marathi identity, invoked by every party.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tiger claws, a basket of sweets, and a crown on a mountain.

spotlights.name: Raigad fort
spotlights.spot_it: A huge flat-topped hill with sheer sides, ruined palace walls, a market street and a stone memorial on top; a ropeway climbs it now.
spotlights.story_md: Shivaji chose Raigad as his capital because three of its sides fall away in cliffs. He was crowned here in 1674 by the priest Gaga Bhatt, who came from Varanasi to perform a ceremony that confirmed his status as a Kshatriya king, against objections from some Brahmins. He died here in April 1680. On the summit are the remains of his palace, a long market street where traders once rode up on horseback, and his samadhi. Beside it is a memorial to a dog, Waghya, said to have jumped onto his master's pyre; historians consider that story a later invention.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the capital of the first Maratha kingdom and a World Heritage component since 2025.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king's capital where only the sky can attack from three sides.

spotlights.name: Pratapgad
spotlights.spot_it: A fort on a forested ridge with layer after layer of blue Sahyadri hills behind it.
spotlights.story_md: Shivaji built Pratapgad in 1656 to guard the passes between the plateau and the Konkan. Three years later it was the stage for the meeting that made his name. Afzal Khan arrived with a large Bijapuri army to finish him; the two met below the fort, alone except for bodyguards. Each side's chroniclers say the other struck first. Shivaji killed Afzal Khan, and his troops, waiting in the forest, routed the army. The battle showed the Maratha way of war: lure a heavy army into thick, steep country and strike it there. Afzal Khan's tomb still stands below the fort.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the turning point that made Shivaji a power, not a rebel.
spotlights.memory_hook: A meeting under a tent that decided the Deccan.

spotlights.name: Sindhudurg sea fort
spotlights.spot_it: Low, zigzag stone walls rising straight out of the sea on a rocky island off Malvan, with a sandy beach inside.
spotlights.story_md: Shivaji understood that whoever held the coast held trade. He built Sindhudurg on a small rocky island off Malvan between 1664 and 1667, to counter the Siddis of Janjira and the Portuguese and English. The walls run about 3 km with more than 40 bastions, and their foundations are said to have been set with molten lead. Inside are fresh water wells, though the fort sits in salt water. A slab of lime holds what is shown as Shivaji's own handprint and footprint, and a shrine inside is one of the few temples dedicated to him. Some families still live inside the walls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the symbol of the Maratha navy, the first serious Indian navy of the modern age.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fort in the sea with sweet water inside.

spotlights.name: Shaniwar Wada
spotlights.spot_it: A massive fortified gate with spiked wooden doors, built against elephants, opening onto empty palace foundations in central Pune.
spotlights.story_md: The Peshwa Bajirao I laid the foundation of this palace on a Saturday in 1730, hence Shaniwar, Saturday. For almost a century the Maratha confederacy was run from here. The spikes on the Delhi Gate were meant to stop war elephants from charging it down. In 1773 the young Peshwa Narayanrao was murdered inside on the orders of his uncle's household; Pune folklore says his ghost still calls 'Kaka, mala vachva' (Uncle, save me) on full-moon nights. In 1828, ten years after the British took Pune, a fire burned for seven days and left only the walls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the seat of the Maratha empire at its widest extent.
spotlights.memory_hook: Saturday's palace: spikes for elephants, a ghost for the tourists.

sections.title: From seven islands to Bombay
sections.intro_md:
In 1661 Portugal handed the islands of Bombay to England as part of the dowry when Catherine of Braganza married Charles II. Seven years later the king leased them to the East India Company for **£10 a year**. At the time they were seven low islands of Koli fishing villages, coconut groves and malarial swamps.

Over the next 150 years the British filled in the gaps. The **Hornby Vellard**, a causeway begun in the 1780s, was the first big project; by the mid-1800s the seven islands had become one. Cotton made the city. When the American Civil War cut off cotton supplies in the 1860s, Bombay's traders made fortunes overnight, and the textile mills of Parel and Girangaon followed. India's first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder to Thane on **16 April 1853**. In 1875 brokers who had traded under a banyan tree formed what became the **Bombay Stock Exchange**, Asia's oldest.

Bombay drew Parsis, Gujaratis, Bohras, Baghdadi Jews and, above all, Marathi workers from the Konkan. The name Mumbai comes from **Mumba Devi**, the goddess of the Koli fisherfolk. The city was officially renamed Mumbai in 1995.

spotlights.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus
spotlights.spot_it: A Gothic railway palace of stone domes, spires and gargoyles, with a statue of Progress on the central dome.
spotlights.story_md: Built as **Victoria Terminus** and named for the Queen's Golden Jubilee in 1887, the station was designed by the British architect F. W. Stevens and took about ten years to build. It mixes Venetian Gothic with Indian details: peacocks, monkeys, gargoyles and carved local faces, many made by students of the Sir J. J. School of Art. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004, and probably the only one that hundreds of thousands of commuters run through every weekday. In 1996 it was renamed after Shivaji, as the city's British names gave way to Marathi ones.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best single building to read Bombay's colonial ambition.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cathedral where the faithful arrive every three minutes by train.

spotlights.name: Gateway of India
spotlights.spot_it: A yellow basalt arch, 26 m high, on the waterfront facing the harbour, with the Taj Mahal Palace hotel behind it.
spotlights.story_md: The Gateway was planned to mark the landing of King George V and Queen Mary in 1911, but it was not finished until 1924, so the king arrived to a cardboard version. Designed by George Wittet, it blends a Roman triumphal arch with Gujarati carving. It became the symbol of empire, and then of its end: on 28 February 1948, the last British troops in India, the 1st Battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry, marched through it to their ships. Today ferries leave from its steps for Elephanta, and its square is Mumbai's most photographed place.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The empire came in through it, and the last of its soldiers left through it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Built for a king who saw only a cardboard copy.

sections.title: The reformers: schools, temples and a new religion
sections.intro_md:
Nineteenth-century Maharashtra produced an unusual run of social reformers, and many of them fought caste and the place of women more than they fought the British.

**Jyotirao Phule**, from a family of gardeners in Pune, and his wife **Savitribai** opened a girls' school in 1848 and later schools for Dalit children, a home for widows' infants and the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873), which rejected Brahmin priests. **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** turned Ganeshotsav into a mass political festival and coined the line 'Swaraj is my birthright'. In the 20th century, **B. R. Ambedkar**, a Mahar from Ratnagiri district, led the Mahad satyagraha of 1927 for the right of untouchables to drink from a public tank, drafted India's Constitution, and in 1956 converted to Buddhism with hundreds of thousands of followers in Nagpur.

That legacy shows in the numbers. In Census 2011, **5.8%** of Maharashtra's people were Buddhist, by far the highest share of any large state, and Phule, Shahu and Ambedkar are named together in politics as the reform tradition of the state.

spotlights.name: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule
spotlights.spot_it: The couple appear together in statues and posters: Jyotirao in a turban and shawl, Savitribai in a sari with her hair pulled back.
spotlights.story_md: In January 1848 the Phules and Sagunabai Kshirsagar opened a girls' school at Bhide Wada in Pune, widely described as the first run by Indians. Savitribai, about 17, became its teacher. On her way to class, people threw stones, mud and cow dung at her, so she carried a second sari to change into at school. By 1851 the couple ran three girls' schools with about 150 pupils. With Fatima Sheikh they taught Muslim and Dalit children too. Savitribai died in the plague of 1897 after carrying a sick boy to a clinic. Her birthday, 3 January, is now marked in Maharashtra as a day for girls' education.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the founders of mass education for girls and lower castes in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A teacher who carried a spare sari to survive the walk to class.

spotlights.name: Ambedkar's conversion at Deekshabhoomi
spotlights.spot_it: A large white hemispherical stupa in Nagpur; on 14 October each year, crowds in white fill the grounds.
spotlights.story_md: On **14 October 1956**, Ashoka Vijaya Dashami, Ambedkar took the Buddhist vows in an open field in Nagpur, then administered them, with 22 vows of his own, to about 400,000 followers, most of them from the Mahar community. It is one of the largest single religious conversions in history. He died less than two months later. The site, Deekshabhoomi, now has a large stupa inaugurated in 2001, and every year on the anniversary hundreds of thousands come. Ambedkar's Navayana Buddhism is why Maharashtra has more Buddhists than any other state.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It changed the religious map of Maharashtra and gave Dalit politics a faith of its own.
spotlights.memory_hook: In one afternoon, 400,000 people changed religion together.

spotlights.name: Anandibai Joshi
spotlights.spot_it: A young woman in a nine-yard Maharashtrian sari and a heavy shawl, photographed in Philadelphia in the 1880s.
spotlights.story_md: Anandibai was married at nine to Gopalrao Joshi, a postal clerk about twenty years older. At 14 she had a son who lived only ten days, for lack of medical care, and she decided to become a doctor. In 1883 she sailed alone to the United States and enrolled at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania. On **11 March 1886** she graduated, with a thesis on obstetrics among Hindus, becoming one of the first Indian women to earn a Western medical degree. She came home to head the women's ward of a Kolhapur hospital, but tuberculosis killed her in February 1887, at 21.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She showed that an Indian woman could be a doctor, a generation before it became normal.
spotlights.memory_hook: Married at nine, a doctor at twenty, gone at twenty-one.

spotlights.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
spotlights.spot_it: A stern man with a thick moustache and a red Puneri pagadi, the turban that became his trademark.
spotlights.story_md: Tilak, a Chitpavan Brahmin from Ratnagiri, ran two newspapers from Pune: Kesari in Marathi and the Mahratta in English. He believed the freedom movement needed the street, not just petitions. In the 1890s he helped turn **Ganeshotsav** and **Shiv Jayanti** into public festivals where nationalist songs and speeches could be heard, gatherings the British could not easily ban. Jailed for sedition, he spent six years in Mandalay prison in Burma, where he wrote Gita Rahasya. His line 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' became the slogan of a generation. He also opposed some social reforms, which reformers held against him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made Indian nationalism a mass movement, and gave Maharashtra its public Ganpati.
spotlights.memory_hook: He turned a home festival into a political rally with a god at its centre.

sections.title: Marathi: a language that won the right to a state
sections.intro_md:
Marathi is the mother tongue of about **8.3 crore** people (2011), third in India after Hindi and Bengali and among the 15 most spoken first languages in the world. It descends from Maharashtri Prakrit, the language of much classical Prakrit poetry. It is written in Devanagari, in a style called Balbodh, but for about 700 years, from the 13th century to the 1950s, clerks and merchants wrote it in **Modi**, a fast cursive script designed so the pen rarely left the paper.

The first great Marathi books were spiritual. In 1290 the teenage saint Dnyaneshwar wrote a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita so ordinary people could read it. The poet-saints Namdev, Eknath and Tukaram followed, and their songs are still sung on the road to Pandharpur.

On **3 October 2024** the Union government declared Marathi a classical language. About 69% of the state speaks it as a first language. Dialects include Varhadi in Vidarbha, Ahirani in Khandesh and Malvani on the southern coast.

spotlights.name: Sant Dnyaneshwar
spotlights.spot_it: Pilgrims in white caps and saffron flags crowd the ghats of the Indrayani river at Alandi, where his samadhi shrine stands.
spotlights.story_md: Dnyaneshwar was the son of a monk who had returned to family life, and the family was outcast by Brahmins for it. At about 16 he dictated the **Dnyaneshwari**, around 9,000 verses explaining the Bhagavad Gita in Marathi, in 1290. It broke the idea that sacred knowledge belonged only to Sanskrit readers. Legend says he made a buffalo recite the Vedas to embarrass the priests. At 21 he entered a chamber at Alandi and sealed himself in, a living samadhi, in 1296. His padukas lead the great wari to Pandharpur every year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the founder of Marathi literature and of the Varkari devotional tradition.
spotlights.memory_hook: A teenager who took the Gita out of Sanskrit and gave it to farmers.

spotlights.name: Modi script
spotlights.spot_it: Flowing, rounded Marathi letters hanging from a top line, with almost no lifts of the pen, on old brown documents.
spotlights.story_md: Modi was the shorthand of power. Its letters were shaped so a clerk could write a whole line without lifting a reed pen, which saved time and ink in a world of handwritten records. The Maratha state, the Peshwas and countless merchants kept their accounts, land records and letters in Modi. After printing took over, the script faded, and it was dropped from schools in the 1950s. Today the Pune archives alone hold an enormous number of Modi documents, and only a small group of trained readers can read them, so a large part of Maratha history is still locked away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Much of Maharashtra's history is written in a script few people can now read.
spotlights.memory_hook: A script built for speed, now slow to read.

sections.title: Faith on foot
sections.intro_md:
Maharashtra's most characteristic religion is not a temple but a road. The **Varkari** tradition worships Vithoba, a form of Krishna who stands on a brick with his hands on his hips at Pandharpur, and its devotees walk there every year, singing the poems of the saints. Varkaris come from every caste; Chokhamela, an untouchable, and Janabai, a maidservant, are among its saints.

Around it, the state is dense with sacred places of every faith. Khandoba at Jejuri is the family god of shepherds, farmers and many Maratha clans, worshipped with clouds of turmeric. Sai Baba of Shirdi, a fakir of uncertain origin who died in 1918, draws Hindus and Muslims alike. The Haji Ali dargah stands in the sea off Worli. Nanded holds one of Sikhism's five takhts, where Guru Gobind Singh died in 1708. The Ashtavinayak circuit links eight Ganesha temples around Pune.

spotlights.name: Pandharpur Wari
spotlights.when: June to July each year, ending on Ashadhi Ekadashi
spotlights.spot_it: Rivers of people in white, women balancing tulsi pots on their heads, men with cymbals and saffron flags, walking and singing on a highway.
spotlights.story_md: Every June, the silver padukas of Dnyaneshwar leave Alandi and those of Tukaram leave Dehu, carried in decorated palanquins. Behind them walk hundreds of thousands of Varkaris, organised into groups called dindis, about 250 km over three weeks, singing abhangs. Along the way, the **ringan** is a high point: a horse runs circles through the crowd, and pilgrims scoop up the dust from its hooves. On Ashadhi Ekadashi they reach Pandharpur, where the Chief Minister performs the official puja. The palkhi custom was started in 1685 by Tukaram's son Narayan Maharaj, and an estimated million people join in some years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the largest annual walking pilgrimages in the world, open to every caste.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three weeks of walking to see a god who stands on a brick.

spotlights.name: Jejuri, the golden temple of Khandoba
spotlights.when: Bhandara festivals on Somvati Amavasya and Champa Shashthi
spotlights.spot_it: A hilltop temple and steps covered in bright yellow turmeric; devotees throwing handfuls of it in clouds.
spotlights.story_md: Khandoba, a warrior form of Shiva on a horse, is the kuladevata (family god) of a huge range of Maharashtrian families, from Dhangar shepherds to Maratha clans. At Jejuri, 50 km from Pune, devotees climb about 200 steps to his temple and throw **bhandar**, turmeric powder, at each other and at the god, so the whole hill turns gold: locals call it Sonyachi Jejuri, Golden Jejuri. Couples come after their weddings to seek blessings. One trial of devotion is lifting a 42 kg sword with the teeth during the Dasara festival.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the folk heart of Maharashtrian Hinduism, older than its textbooks.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god so loved he is buried in turmeric.

spotlights.name: Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib
spotlights.when: Guru Gobind Singh died here in 1708
spotlights.spot_it: A white and gold gurdwara beside the Godavari in Nanded, with a gilded dome.
spotlights.story_md: In 1708 the tenth Sikh Guru, **Gobind Singh**, travelled south with the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah and settled at Nanded on the Godavari. Here he declared that after him the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the eternal Guru. He was stabbed by assassins and died at Nanded. The gurdwara built on the spot, rebuilt under Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the 1830s, is one of the **five takhts**, the seats of Sikh authority. Its Deccani Sikh community has its own customs, distinct from Punjab's.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes Maharashtra one of the holiest places in Sikhism.
spotlights.memory_hook: The line of human Gurus ended on the banks of the Godavari.

sections.title: Lavani, drums and the birth of Indian cinema
sections.intro_md:
Maharashtra's performing arts run on two tracks. One is folk and loud: **Lavani** and **Tamasha** troupes touring the villages, **powada** ballads about Shivaji's battles, the Koli fishing dances of the coast, and the huge drum troupes of Pune. The other is urban and polished: Marathi sangeet natak (musical theatre), which began with Vishnudas Bhave's Sita Swayamvar in Sangli in 1843, and Hindustani classical music, with the Kirana and Gwalior traditions strong in Pune; Bhimsen Joshi's Sawai Gandharva festival there is one of India's oldest.

Then there is film. India's first full-length feature film was made in Bombay in 1913 by a man from Nashik, and Mumbai has been the centre of Hindi cinema ever since. Marathi cinema has its own long line, from the Prabhat studios of the 1930s to Sairat (2016), the first Marathi film to earn over ₹100 crore. Lata Mangeshkar, the most famous voice in Indian music, grew up singing Marathi stage songs.

spotlights.name: Lavani
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a tight nine-yard sari worn like trousers, heavy jewellery, stamping fast to a dholki drum, with sharp flicks of the hips and a teasing gaze at the audience.
spotlights.story_md: Lavani grew up in the 18th and 19th centuries around Maratha army camps and the Peshwa court, and later with travelling Tamasha troupes. The dancer wears the **nauvari**, a nine-yard sari draped between the legs, which lets her move freely. The rhythm is set by the dholki and ankle bells, and the songs range from devotional to openly flirtatious. Phadachi Lavani is performed on a public stage; Baithakichi Lavani is sung seated for a small audience. Many performers came from the Kolhati and other marginalised communities and faced stigma. Stars such as Surekha Punekar and films like Natarang (2010) brought it respectability on TV and film.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Maharashtra's signature folk performance, and its most argued about.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine yards of sari, one dholki, no apologies.

spotlights.name: Lata Mangeshkar
spotlights.spot_it: A small woman in a white sari with a red border, hair in a long plait, standing very still at the microphone.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Indore in 1929 to Deenanath Mangeshkar, a Marathi stage singer and actor, Lata began singing in films at 13 after her father's death to support her family. Over seven decades she recorded in more than 36 languages and became the voice of Hindi film heroines from the 1950s onwards. On 27 January 1963 she sang **'Ae Mere Watan Ke Logon'** for the soldiers of the 1962 war, and Nehru is said to have wept. She received the Bharat Ratna in 2001. She died in Mumbai on 6 February 2022, and her ashes were scattered in the Godavari at Nashik.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the most widely heard voice in Indian history.
spotlights.memory_hook: Her father's Marathi stage gave India its film voice.

spotlights.name: Dadasaheb Phalke and Raja Harishchandra
spotlights.spot_it: A man with a moustache and round glasses; a grainy black-and-white still of a king and queen in a forest set.
spotlights.story_md: Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, born in Trimbak in 1870, was a printer and magician who saw a film about the life of Christ and decided Indian gods needed films too. He went to London to buy a camera, then shot **Raja Harishchandra** in Bombay with his family's savings. No woman would act, so a male cook, Anna Salunke, played the queen. It opened at the Coronation Cinema in Girgaon on 3 May 1913 and is counted as India's first full-length feature film. Phalke made about 95 features and 27 shorts, then died poor in Nashik in 1944. India's top film award has carried his name since 1969.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the start of the world's most prolific film industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's first film heroine was a man who worked in a restaurant kitchen.

sections.title: Silk, rice paste and buffalo leather
sections.intro_md:
Three crafts carry Maharashtra's name around the world, and each comes from a different layer of society. The **Paithani** sari is court silk, woven with real gold and silver thread in Paithan and Yeola, once worn by Peshwa families. **Warli** painting comes from the Adivasi villages of the northern Konkan, where women painted it on mud walls for weddings. The **Kolhapuri** chappal comes from the leatherworkers of the south, mostly Dalit artisans, and is now copied by luxury brands.

All three hold Geographical Indication tags, and all three face the same problem: cheap machine-made copies sell for a fraction of the price while the real makers struggle to earn. Other crafts to know are the Himroo shawls of Aurangabad, the wooden toys of Sawantwadi and the Bidri-style metal inlay of the Deccan. The **nauvari**, the nine-yard sari draped like trousers, is the dress of Lavani dancers, Koli women and brides, and of Maratha women who once rode horses in it.

visual.title: Paithani vs Warli: court and village

rows.Paithani: Handloom weavers in Yeola and Paithan

spotlights.name: Paithani sari
spotlights.spot_it: A silk sari with a broad gold border and a pallu woven with peacocks or lotus vines; the colour changes when the cloth moves.
spotlights.story_md: A true Paithani is woven on a handloom with silk and zari, and its pallu (the decorated end) is made by a slow tapestry technique in which each colour is interlocked by hand. The signature motifs are the peacock (mor), the lotus and the asawali flowering vine. Weaving one can take months, sometimes up to two years for the most complex designs, which is why prices start around ₹20,000 and go into lakhs. The craft is named after Paithan, the old Satavahana capital, but most Paithanis today come from **Yeola** in Nashik district, which has thousands of weavers. Power-loom copies sell for a tenth of the price.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Maharashtrian bride's sari and the state's grandest textile.
spotlights.memory_hook: A peacock that takes a year to weave.

spotlights.name: Warli painting
spotlights.when: Ancient tradition; on paper since the 1970s
spotlights.spot_it: White stick figures of circles and triangles dancing in a spiral on a red-brown wall.
spotlights.story_md: Warli art uses only three shapes: the circle (sun and moon), the triangle (mountains and trees) and the square (a sacred enclosure). People are two triangles joined at the tip. It is painted in white rice paste on walls of mud and cow dung by Warli women, traditionally for weddings, inside the **chauk**, a square frame around the mother goddess. The most famous motif is the **tarpa dance**, a spiral of dancers around a musician blowing a gourd trumpet. In the 1970s **Jivya Soma Mashe** began painting it on paper as art, and it is now everywhere from railway stations to T-shirts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of India's best-known tribal art forms, and a lesson in minimal design.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole world drawn with three shapes and rice.

spotlights.name: Kolhapuri chappal
spotlights.spot_it: Flat open sandals of tan buffalo leather with a toe loop and a broad strap, often with a braided or punched pattern and no nails.
spotlights.story_md: Kolhapuris are made by hand from vegetable-tanned buffalo leather, stitched with leather thread and no nails; a heavy pair for farm work can weigh far more than a city pair. The rulers of Kolhapur promoted the craft and opened tanning centres for it. In June 2025 **Prada** showed nearly identical sandals in its Milan menswear show, labelled only as leather sandals. After an outcry in India and a complaint from a Maharashtra chamber of commerce, Prada acknowledged the Indian inspiration and sent a team to meet Kolhapur artisans. A pair in Kolhapur costs a few hundred rupees.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a GI craft now at the centre of the global argument over cultural copying.
spotlights.memory_hook: Prada's new sandal was a Kolhapuri old enough to have a GI tag.

sections.title: From vada pav to Malvani fish
sections.intro_md:
There is no single Maharashtrian food. The **Konkan** coast eats rice, coconut and fish: bombil (Bombay duck), surmai and pomfret in red coconut curries, finished with pink **sol kadhi**. The **Desh** plateau around Pune and Kolhapur eats jowar and bajra bhakri, fiery mutton in red and white gravies (tambda and pandhra rassa), and sweet-sour dals with jaggery. **Vidarbha** has the hottest food in the state, saoji mutton from Nagpur. And Mumbai invented its own street food out of the needs of mill workers who had five minutes and five rupees.

Across the state, a home meal follows a pattern: rice, a bhaji, a thin varan dal, chapati or bhakri, a koshimbir salad and a pickle, often with a dollop of ghee on the rice. Festivals have their own dishes: puran poli at Holi, modak for Ganpati, shrikhand at Gudi Padwa. The state also grows the most famous mango in India, most of India's grapes, and its oranges come from Nagpur.

spotlights.name: Vada pav
spotlights.spot_it: A fried, gram-flour-coated potato ball in a soft square bun, with dry red garlic chutney and a fried green chilli on the side.
spotlights.story_md: Mumbai's burger is usually credited to **Ashok Vaidya**, who opened a stall outside Dadar station in 1966 to feed mill workers on the move; others name Sudhakar Mhatre or the Khidki stall in Kalyan. The bun, pav, came with the Portuguese; the batata vada is pure Maharashtrian. When the mills closed in the 1970s and 1980s, the Shiv Sena encouraged laid-off Marathi workers to open vada pav stalls, and the snack became a political symbol. It still costs about ₹15 to ₹25 on most streets. 23 August is now marked as World Vada Pav Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the fuel of Mumbai, and the cheapest full meal in the city.
spotlights.memory_hook: A potato that fed the mills, then fed the Shiv Sena.

spotlights.name: Ukadiche modak
spotlights.spot_it: White, pleated, onion-shaped rice dumplings with a pointed top, served with a spoon of ghee.
spotlights.story_md: The modak is said to be Ganesha's favourite sweet, so it is made in almost every Maharashtrian home during Ganeshotsav, often 21 at a time as an offering. The shell is a soft steamed rice-flour dough (ukad means steamed); the filling is fresh coconut and jaggery with cardamom. The skill is in the pleats: a good cook makes 11 to 21 even folds pinched to a point. A broken modak in the steamer is a small family disgrace. Fried modaks and mawa modaks from sweet shops exist, but the steamed one is the classic.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the food of Maharashtra's biggest festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-one pleats for the elephant god.

spotlights.name: Malvani thali and sol kadhi
spotlights.spot_it: A steel plate with red coconut curry, fried fish or chicken, rice, vade and a small bowl of pale pink drink.
spotlights.story_md: On the southern Konkan coast, the cooking is Malvani: fresh coconut roasted dark with red chillies and a dozen spices into a masala for fish, prawns or chicken, eaten with rice or with **vade**, puffy fried bread. Every meal ends with **sol kadhi**, a pink drink made of coconut milk and kokum, the sour purple fruit of a coastal tree, with garlic and green chilli. It cools the mouth after the heat and is said to aid digestion. Bombil fry, with the soft Bombay duck fish flattened and coated in rava, is the coastal favourite.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the taste of the Konkan, which much of Mumbai's Marathi population came from.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pink drink, red curry, the sea on a plate.

spotlights.name: Alphonso (Hapus) mango
spotlights.when: Season late March to June; GI tag 2018
spotlights.spot_it: A medium, egg-shaped mango with a golden skin blushed red at the top, saffron flesh, and a scent you notice across a room.
spotlights.story_md: The Alphonso is named after **Afonso de Albuquerque**, the Portuguese commander who took Goa in 1510; the Portuguese are credited with grafting mango trees on this coast. In Marathi it is **hapus**. The best, by local agreement, come from Ratnagiri and Devgad on the laterite slopes of the Konkan, which got a GI tag in 2018. Fruit is sold by the dozen, and prices at the start of the season can reach several thousand rupees a dozen. The US banned Indian mangoes from 1989 to 2007, and the EU briefly in 2014, over fruit flies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's most famous mango and a major Konkan export.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Portuguese general's name on India's best mango.

spotlights.name: Nashik wine
spotlights.spot_it: Neat rows of vines on gentle slopes outside Nashik, with the Sahyadri hills behind.
spotlights.story_md: Nashik was famous for table grapes long before wine. Its dry winters and basalt soils at about 600 m suit vines, and the district grows a large share of India's export grapes. In 1999 **Rajeev Samant**, a Stanford graduate who had worked at Oracle in California, returned to his family land and founded Sula Vineyards, planting Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc. Sula became India's largest wine brand and the region now has dozens of wineries. Maharashtra's policy treats wine as a farm product to help growers, which also makes it politically touchy. Nashik calls itself India's wine capital.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the centre of India's modern wine industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: A software man came home and planted Sauvignon Blanc among the grapes.

sections.title: Ganpati, gudi and bullocks
sections.intro_md:
The festival calendar follows the farming year. **Gudi Padwa** in March or April opens the Marathi new year. **Ashadhi Ekadashi** in June or July ends the wari. **Narali Purnima** in August reopens the sea for the Kolis. **Pola**, at the end of the Shravan month, honours the bullocks that plough the fields. Then comes the biggest of all, **Ganeshotsav**, ten days in August or September, followed by Navratri, Dasara and Diwali, and Makar Sankranti in January, when people swap til-gul sweets and say 'til-gul ghya, god god bola' (take the sesame-jaggery and speak sweetly).

On 10 July 2025 the state government declared Ganeshotsav an official state festival. Shiv Jayanti, Shivaji's birthday on 19 February, and Ambedkar Jayanti on 14 April are among the largest public celebrations in the state. Every 12 years, Nashik and Trimbakeshwar host the Simhastha Kumbh Mela, due next in 2027.

spotlights.name: Ganeshotsav and Lalbaugcha Raja
spotlights.when: Ten days in August or September; Lalbaug pandal since 1934
spotlights.spot_it: A giant Ganesha idol, several metres high, crowned and seated on a throne in a crowded pandal; later carried to the sea in a sea of red gulal.
spotlights.story_md: Most homes install a small clay Ganesha for 1.5, 5, 7 or 11 days. Public mandals install huge ones. Bal Gangadhar Tilak and others turned the festival into a public event in the 1890s. The most famous mandal is **Lalbaugcha Raja**, started in 1934 by fishermen and traders in the mill district. Its idol is so popular that queues for darshan can run for 20 to 30 hours, and celebrities line up beside mill workers. On Anant Chaturdashi the idols are carried to the sea at Girgaon Chowpatty with drums and dancing, and the visarjan of Lalbaug's idol can take more than 20 hours. Around 150,000 idols are immersed in Mumbai each year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the defining public festival of Maharashtra, made an official state festival in 2025.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queue of 24 hours to see a god for 2 seconds.

spotlights.name: Gudi Padwa
spotlights.when: Chaitra Shukla Pratipada, March or April
spotlights.spot_it: A bamboo pole outside a window, topped with an upturned copper or silver pot over a bright silk cloth, with a neem sprig and a garland of sugar crystals.
spotlights.story_md: On the first day of the Hindu month of Chaitra, Maharashtrian homes raise a **gudi**: a pole draped with a new cloth, topped by an upturned pot, and hung with neem leaves, mango leaves, flowers and a garland of white sugar crystals (gathi). It marks the new year and is said to recall Rama's return to Ayodhya, or Shalivahana's victory. Families eat bitter neem with jaggery, for a year of both. In recent decades, cities such as Dombivli, Girgaon and Thane have added huge morning processions, called shobha yatras, with women on motorbikes in nauvari saris and pheta turbans.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Marathi new year and a public show of Marathi identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: A flag of silk, sugar and neem for the new year.

spotlights.name: Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Simhastha Kumbh 2027
spotlights.spot_it: A stone ghat on the Godavari at Nashik, crowded with bathers; in 2026, the river bed dry while new ghats are built.
spotlights.story_md: The Kumbh Mela rotates between Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik, roughly every 12 years at each. At Nashik it is called **Simhastha** because it falls when Jupiter is in Leo (Simha). Its unusual feature is that it has two centres: the Vaishnava akharas bathe at **Ramkund** in Nashik and the Shaiva akharas at Kushavarta in Trimbak, 30 km away. The next Simhastha is due from mid-2027. By May 2026 the river at Ramkund had been drained for new ghats and works. It is where Lata Mangeshkar's ashes were immersed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the biggest event Maharashtra will host in 2027.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jupiter enters Leo and Nashik fills up.

sections.title: How Maharashtra lives
sections.intro_md:
Half the state lives in towns and cities, and the other half in villages whose life follows the monsoon. Mumbai is the extreme: about 2 crore people in the metropolitan region, a city where the average commute is long and the train is the lifeline, and where perhaps four in ten people live in slums or chawls (estimates vary widely).

Pune is known for dry, sharp humour and the **Puneri patya**, blunt shop signs such as 'Do not ask for change, we will not give it'. Many Marathi families skip meat on certain days or through the month of Shravan. Cricket is played on any flat ground, and kho-kho and kabaddi are school favourites.

Rural Maharashtra lives with two hard facts: much of the land is unirrigated, and for years the state has recorded more farmer suicides than any other in the national crime records, concentrated in the cotton districts of Vidarbha and Marathwada.

spotlights.name: Mumbai local trains
spotlights.spot_it: A packed electric train with people hanging out of open doors, rushing past a platform in a blur of shirts and saris.
spotlights.story_md: Mumbai's suburban trains carry somewhere between 6 and 7.5 million passengers a day on about 450 km of track, in more than 2,300 services. At peak hours a 12-car train meant for about 2,000 can hold over 4,500, a crush load of 14 to 16 standing people per square metre. There are ladies' compartments, first class, and now AC trains. Regular commuters have unwritten rules: who gets the 'fourth seat' at the edge of a bench, where to stand to get off at your station. The cost is human: from 2002 to 2012, an average of about 3,700 people died on the tracks each year, falling from trains or crossing lines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the circulation system of India's financial capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A train built for 2,000 that carries 4,500.

spotlights.name: Mumbai's dabbawalas
spotlights.spot_it: Men in white Gandhi caps and kurtas with long wooden crates of tiffin boxes balanced on their heads or bicycles, outside a railway station.
spotlights.story_md: Every working day about 5,000 dabbawalas collect home-cooked lunches in steel tiffins from homes across Mumbai, carry them by train, bicycle and handcart to offices, and bring the empty boxes back in the afternoon. They move about 200,000 tiffins a day. Each box carries a code of letters, numbers and colours for the station, building and floor, because many dabbawalas had little schooling. The service was started in 1890 by **Mahadeo Havaji Bachche**. Most dabbawalas are Varkaris from villages near Pune. Their famous error rate, about one mistake in several million deliveries, is a union estimate, not an audit, and they were never certified Six Sigma.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a logistics system admired by business schools and built without computers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lunch goes to work by train, and comes home empty.

spotlights.name: Dharavi
spotlights.when: Grew from a Koli village from the 1880s
spotlights.spot_it: A dense maze of low buildings, tin roofs and narrow lanes in the middle of Mumbai, with workshops on every ground floor.
spotlights.story_md: Dharavi covers about 2.1 to 2.4 km² between the city's two railway lines and has somewhere between 700,000 and a million residents; nobody knows exactly. It is often called Asia's largest slum, which is a contested title. What surprises visitors is work: leather goods, pottery in the Kumbharwada potters' quarter, garments, food and above all recycling, from plastic to metal. Its informal economy is estimated at US$500 million to over $1 billion a year. A redevelopment project led by the Adani Group, which won the tender in 2022 and survived a court challenge in December 2024, aims to rebuild it; residents are divided.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most debated square kilometre of urban India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A slum with a billion-dollar economy.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
A short list from a long roster. Beyond the names in earlier sections (Shivaji, the Phules, Ambedkar, Tilak, Lata, Phalke), Maharashtra gave India **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**, Gandhi's political mentor; **Vinoba Bhave**, who walked the country asking landlords to give land to the landless; the physicist **Homi Bhabha**, founder of India's atomic programme in Mumbai; **Dhondo Keshav Karve**, who founded India's first women's university; the novelist **P. L. Deshpande**, still the most-quoted humorist in Marathi; the Hindustani vocalist **Bhimsen Joshi**; and the economist **D. R. Gadgil**, who helped design the cooperative sugar movement.

In sport and business, two names stand above the rest. One is a cricketer from a middle-class Bandra colony. The other led a business group founded in Bombay in 1868 that now runs from salt to software.

spotlights.name: Sachin Tendulkar
spotlights.spot_it: A short, curly-haired batsman with a heavy bat, a straight drive played with his head perfectly still.
spotlights.story_md: Tendulkar grew up in Bandra and learned the game at Shivaji Park under coach **Ramakant Achrekar**, who placed a one-rupee coin on the stumps for anyone who could get him out. He made his Test debut in Karachi in 1989 at 16. Over 24 years he played 200 Tests and 463 ODIs, scored 100 international centuries, and in 2010 became the first man to score a double century in an ODI. He won the 2011 World Cup at the Wankhede Stadium, his home ground. He retired in 2013 and received the Bharat Ratna in 2014, the first sportsperson to get it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the most famous Indian of his generation and the measure of Indian cricket.
spotlights.memory_hook: A one-rupee coin on the stumps built 100 hundreds.

spotlights.name: Ratan Tata and the House of Tata
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, quiet man with silver hair and glasses; behind him, the red domes of the Taj Mahal Palace hotel on the Mumbai waterfront.
spotlights.story_md: Jamsetji Tata founded the group in Bombay in 1868 and opened the **Taj Mahal Palace** hotel in 1903, a story says because he was refused entry to a whites-only hotel; historians doubt the tale. His successors built steel, power, airlines and software from Bombay House in Fort. **Ratan Tata** ran the group from 1991 to 2012, bought Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley, launched the Nano, and became the most admired businessman in India. The Taj was attacked in the 26 November 2008 terror attacks and reopened within weeks. He died on 9 October 2024; Mumbai lined the streets for his funeral.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Tata group is the clearest example of Bombay capital building modern India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hotel with domes, a car for one lakh, and a city in mourning.

sections.title: How Maharashtra earns
sections.intro_md:
Maharashtra is India's economic engine, and the engine is lopsided. Services make up well over half the state's output: banking, insurance, the stock exchanges, the RBI headquarters, film and media in Mumbai; IT and education in Pune. Industry follows: cars and two-wheelers around Pune, chemicals and pharma near Thane, engineering in Nashik and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. The **JNPA** port across the harbour from Mumbai has been India's busiest container port for most of the last 25 years, and a new deep-water port at **Vadhavan** in Palghar is being built to handle some of the world's largest ships.

Farming employs nearly half the workforce but adds a small share of output. Sugarcane is king in the west, grown by powerful **cooperative sugar factories** that also make politicians: the first was set up at Pravaranagar in 1950. Cotton and soybean dominate Vidarbha and Marathwada, where rain fails often. Maharashtra's 2026-27 budget puts GSDP at about ₹54 lakh crore and spends ₹26,500 crore on the Ladki Bahin scheme, monthly cash for women.

The visible story of the 2020s is infrastructure: the Samruddhi expressway to Nagpur, metro lines, a sea bridge and a second airport.

spotlights.name: Atal Setu (Mumbai Trans Harbour Link)
spotlights.spot_it: A six-lane road bridge running straight across open sea for kilometres, with orange-lit sections and flamingos in the mudflats below.
spotlights.story_md: The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link, named Atal Setu after Atal Bihari Vajpayee, runs about 21.8 km from Sewri in Mumbai to Chirle near Navi Mumbai, with about 16.5 km over the sea. It is India's longest sea bridge. It cut the drive from south Mumbai to the mainland from up to two hours to around 20 minutes. It cost about ₹17,843 crore and used enough steel, the builders said, for 17 Eiffel Towers. Engineers fitted noise barriers and special lighting so the flamingos that winter on the Sewri mudflats would not be disturbed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties Mumbai to the mainland and to its new airport.
spotlights.memory_hook: A road across the sea with noise barriers for flamingos.

spotlights.name: Navi Mumbai International Airport
spotlights.spot_it: A terminal roof shaped like an opening lotus, with long white petals, beside new runways on reclaimed land.
spotlights.story_md: Mumbai's old airport at Santacruz is one of the busiest single-runway airports in the world and has no room to grow. The answer took nearly 30 years: a new airport across the harbour in Navi Mumbai, on land that included hills flattened and a river diverted. Prime Minister Modi inaugurated it on 8 October 2025, and commercial flights began on 25 December 2025. The terminal, designed by Zaha Hadid Architects, takes the lotus as its motif. Phase one handles about 20 million passengers a year; the plan is 90 million. It is run by an Adani-led company with the state agency CIDCO.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives Mumbai the second airport it has needed for decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lotus-shaped airport on a flattened hill.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Follow the rock first: Ajanta and Ellora from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (two days), Elephanta by ferry from the Gateway, Karla near Lonavala. Then the forts: Raigad by ropeway, Pratapgad from Mahabaleshwar, Sinhagad from Pune, Sindhudurg by boat from Malvan. For the coast, the Konkan from Alibaug to Tarkarli has quiet beaches, Ganpatipule's seaside temple and the best Malvani food. Matheran bans cars and is reached by a toy train. Go to Kaas in September, Tadoba from March to June, Bhigwan in winter for flamingos.

In the cities: Mumbai's Fort and Kala Ghoda for Victorian Gothic, Marine Drive for Art Deco, and the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya museum; Pune's Shaniwar Wada and the Aga Khan Palace, where Gandhi was held from 1942 to 1944 and Kasturba died; Nagpur for Deekshabhoomi. October to February suits most of the state; the monsoon is the season for the Ghats.

sections.title: What is happening now (2024 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**Politics.** In the November 2024 election the BJP-led Mahayuti won 235 of 288 seats; the BJP alone won 132. **Devendra Fadnavis**, from Nagpur, returned as Chief Minister on 5 December 2024, after serving as deputy under Eknath Shinde. On 28 January 2026 Deputy Chief Minister **Ajit Pawar** was killed when his plane crashed while landing at Baramati; his wife Sunetra Pawar took his place.

**Mumbai.** In the long-delayed civic election of 15 January 2026, the BJP won 89 of 227 seats and, with Shinde's Shiv Sena, ended the Thackeray family's long hold on the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation. The BJP's Ritu Tawde became mayor.

**Identity.** Marathi became a classical language in October 2024. In 2025 an order making Hindi a compulsory third language in primary schools was withdrawn after protests that put Uddhav and Raj Thackeray on one stage. Manoj Jarange's Mumbai fast for Maratha quota benefits ended on 2 September 2025 when the government accepted his demand.

**Building.** Twelve Maratha forts became a World Heritage Site in July 2025, Navi Mumbai airport opened to flights on 25 December 2025, and Nashik is preparing for the 2027 Kumbh.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
**'Mumbai is Maharashtra.'** Mumbai makes up a large share of the state's output, but most Maharashtrians live far from it, and Vidarbha and Marathwada feel ignored enough that a separate Vidarbha state is a live demand.

**'Everyone in Mumbai speaks Marathi.'** Marathi is the mother tongue of only about a third of Greater Mumbai's people in Census 2011; Hindi, Urdu and Gujarati are large. That gap drives the city's language politics.

**'The dabbawalas are Six Sigma certified.'** They are not. The error figure comes from a union estimate repeated by the press.

**'Shivaji was anti-Muslim.'** Historians generally describe his religious policy as tolerant: he had Muslim commanders and naval officers, and his enemies included Hindu generals in Mughal service. His legacy is contested in modern politics, not in his own time.

**'Maharashtra means great nation.'** Possibly. Other theories link it to the Rashtrakuta dynasty, to a tribe called Maharathi, or to Mahars. The origin is uncertain.

**Recap.** Lava hills facing the sea; India's finest cave art; a kingdom built on forts; a colonial port turned financial capital; reformers who took on caste; a language that won a state; and an economy so large its gaps are just as large.

side_dish.title: The Deccan Traps: the lava that may have helped end the dinosaurs
side_dish.body_md:
Every hill you saw today, from Raigad to the Ellora cliff, is made of the same thing: basalt from the Deccan Traps. 'Trap' comes from the Swedish word for stairs, after the step-like hills the lava layers make.

About 66 million years ago, cracks in the Earth's crust over a hotspot (the same one now under Réunion island) poured out lava again and again, for hundreds of thousands of years. The flows piled up more than 2 km thick in places and covered perhaps 1.5 million km², an area larger than Maharashtra four times over.

The timing is the interesting part. The eruptions peaked close to the moment the Chicxulub asteroid hit Mexico and the dinosaurs died out. The volcanoes released enormous amounts of carbon dioxide and sulphur gases, which changed the climate. Geologists still argue about how much of the mass extinction was the asteroid, how much was the Deccan, and whether the impact may have intensified the eruptions. Most now think both played a part.

For Maharashtra the legacy is practical. Basalt is hard but carves evenly, which is why it holds Ajanta and Ellora. It breaks into flat-topped hills with cliffs, which is why Shivaji could defend a kingdom with forts. It weathers into black cotton soil, which is why Vidarbha grows cotton. And it holds water poorly, which is why so much of the plateau faces drought.

offline_task.title: Make kanda poha, Maharashtra's breakfast, tomorrow morning
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2. 20 minutes.** Poha is the breakfast of Pune and Nagpur, eaten at home, at office canteens and at every railway station.

**You need**
- 2 cups thick poha (flattened rice)
- 1 onion, finely chopped; 1 small potato, diced small (optional)
- 2 green chillies, slit; a sprig of curry leaves
- 2 tablespoons peanuts
- Half a teaspoon each of mustard seeds and cumin, a quarter teaspoon of turmeric, a pinch of hing
- 1 teaspoon sugar, salt, juice of half a lemon
- Fresh coriander and grated coconut to finish

**Method**
1. Rinse the poha in a sieve under running water for 20 seconds, until soft but not mushy. Let it drain. Sprinkle the sugar, salt and turmeric over it and mix gently with your fingers.
2. Heat 2 tablespoons of oil. Fry the peanuts until golden, then lift them out.
3. In the same oil, add mustard seeds; when they crackle add cumin, hing, curry leaves and chillies. Add the onion (and potato, if using) and cook until the onion is soft.
4. Add the poha and peanuts. Toss on low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, covered for the last minute so it steams.
5. Take off the heat, squeeze over lemon, and top with coriander and coconut. In Indore and Nagpur they add a handful of crunchy sev on top.

Eat it with a cup of strong, sweet chai, the way most of Maharashtra starts its day.
